391.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
391.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that knowing the Truth is supreme, but living it out in one's conduct ranks higher still.
391.tie_back: The Kural asks us to learn flawlessly and then to stand by what we have learned; Guru Nanak places conduct that matches the truth above knowledge of it, which is the second half of the couplet.
391.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
391._accuracy_note: Strong fit on living by what one knows; the verse speaks of Truth (God and the Name) rather than of learning as such, and does not address learning without flaw.

392.quote_or_event: Guru Angad, the second Sikh Guru, is remembered as the standardizer of the Gurmukhi script in which much of the Adi Granth is written, and Sikh tradition credits him with setting up schools to teach young people to read and write in their own language, Punjabi, rather than classical Sanskrit.
392.explanation: By fixing a script for the people's own language, Guru Angad made literacy and direct access to the Gurus' hymns possible for ordinary Sikhs.
392.tie_back: The Kural calls letters and numbers the two eyes of every living person; Guru Angad's work on Gurmukhi and the schools linked to him reflect the same conviction that basic literacy belongs to everyone.
392._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it concerns letters only, not numbers, and Britannica presents the schools as Sikh tradition ('Sikh lore') while stating the standardization of Gurmukhi as fact.

393.quote_or_event: “Do not call them blind, who have no eyes in their face. They alone are blind, O Nanak, who wander away from their Lord and Master.”
393.explanation: In a salok in Ramkali ki Vaar Guru Angad redefines blindness: the truly blind are not those without physical sight but those who have strayed from the Lord.
393.tie_back: The Kural says only the learned truly have eyes and the unlearned merely carry two sores on their face; Guru Angad makes the same move of denying that physical eyes are real sight.
393.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
393._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel; for Guru Angad true sight comes from closeness to the Lord rather than from learning, and the verse is gentler toward the physically blind than the Kural's image.

394.quote_or_event: “The sight of them banishes my evil-mindedness; they are my only true friends.”
394.explanation: In a salok of Gujri ki Vaar Guru Arjan says his true friends are those whose very presence drives away his bad thoughts.
394.tie_back: The Kural defines the learned by the gladness people feel on meeting them and the longing they feel on parting; Guru Arjan likewise names his true friends by the good their mere presence works in him.
394.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 520, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
394._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the friends meant are the Guru's devotees rather than scholars, and the verse does not mention the longing to meet again after parting.

395.quote_or_event: “Bowing down, again and again, I fall at the Feet of my Guru; through Him, I have seen the Lord, the Divine Self, within.”
395.explanation: Guru Nanak describes humbly bowing again and again before the Guru, through whose teaching he came to see the Lord within himself.
395.tie_back: The Kural says those who stand humbly before their teachers, like the needy before the rich, are truly superior; Guru Nanak shows the same humility before the teacher as the way to the highest understanding.
395.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 353, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
395._accuracy_note: Strong fit on humility before the teacher; in Sikhism the Guru is the spiritual guide to God rather than a teacher of learning in general, and the verse does not condemn those who will not learn.

396.quote_or_event: “The seeker comes forth, and the debater dies down; I am a sacrifice, a sacrifice to the Guru, the Creator Lord.”
396.explanation: Guru Nanak says that the one who keeps searching grows in spiritual life, while the one who only argues withers away.
396.tie_back: The Kural says understanding wells up in proportion to how deeply one digs into learning; Guru Nanak likewise says that it is the persistent seeker, not the disputer, who comes to flourish.
396.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1255, Raag Malaar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
396._accuracy_note: Next-best only: seeking that bears fruit is the shared idea, but Gurbani gives no matching image of growth in proportion to depth, and its search is for God, not for learning.

397.quote_or_event: “No one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. I get along with everyone.”
397.explanation: Guru Arjan says that since he found the company of the holy, no one seems an enemy or a stranger to him and he is at home with all.
397.tie_back: The Kural says that to the learned every land and every town becomes their own; Guru Arjan describes the same freedom from foreignness, in which no one is a stranger.
397.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1299, Raag Kaanraa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
397._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the universal belonging is the shared idea, but in the hymn it comes from the company of the holy (sadh sangat), not from learning.

398.quote_or_event: “Where there is no mother, father, children, friends or siblings - O my mind, there, only the Naam, the Name of the Lord, shall be with you as your help and support.”
398.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan says that where no family or friend can follow, beyond this life, only the Name goes with a person as their support.
398.tie_back: The Kural says learning gained in one life protects a person through seven lives to come; Guru Arjan names the Naam as the one possession that goes with the soul beyond this life and keeps protecting it.
398.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib (Ashtpadi 2), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
398._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both speak of a support that lasts beyond this life, but for Guru Arjan it is the Name, not learning, and he does not speak of seven births.

399.quote_or_event: “Contemplate and reflect upon knowledge, and you will become a benefactor to others.”
399.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that knowledge truly reflected upon makes a person a benefactor of others (paropkari).
399.tie_back: The Kural says the learned love learning more when they see it delight the whole world; Guru Nanak likewise sees the proof of real learning in the good it does for others.
399.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
399._accuracy_note: Strong fit on learning that benefits the world; Guru Nanak stresses service to others rather than the learner's growing delight in learning.

400.quote_or_event: “The Siblings of Destiny meet together, and eat and spend, but these resources do not diminish; they continue to increase.”
400.explanation: Guru Arjan speaks of the spiritual treasure of the Name: however much those who gather in holy company use and share it, it never runs out and only grows.
400.tie_back: The Kural calls learning the one imperishable wealth beside which nothing else is wealth; Guru Arjan describes a spiritual treasure with the same quality of never being used up.
400.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 186, Raag Gauree, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
400._accuracy_note: Strong fit on an inexhaustible, ever-growing wealth; the treasure is the Name and devotion, not learning, and the line does not dismiss other possessions as the Kural does.
